title: After Automation: AI progress creates more work for humans, not less
author: Dan Shipper

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution against inferring immediate displacement from capability gains by observing expanding human workloads among AI developers and early adopters. However, it also predicts near-term superhuman, day-scale autonomous AI and leaves open whether the current workload expansion is merely temporary, creating substantive uncertainty about the cluster’s emphasis on reconfiguration rather than replacement.
qs: If you talk to anyone in the AI industry—or to early adopters outside of it—you’ll hear the same thing we’ve noticed internally: There’s more work to do than ever.
It seems that we are on the cusp of an AI smarter than any human, with the autonomy to work for almost a full day at a time.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Shipper accepts the cluster’s core account of selective task automation, human oversight and work redesign, then materially develops it through the “frame versus framer” distinction: benchmark success within bounded tasks does not establish general competence or eliminate human goal-setting and judgment. Every’s experience also supplies a concrete, though non-legal and organisation-specific, example of automation generating new review, evaluation and workflow demands. His AGI claims are predictions rather than direct evidence and do not displace his near-term augmentation thesis.
qs: The score tells us how well the model operates inside a frame we supplied; it does not tell us that the model has become us.

Some use AI to build systems that absorb and leverage the flood of new work: review queues, evals, harnesses, repo rules, Claude and Codex instruction files, continuous integration (CI), permissions, and workflows that turn first attempts into great work.

kp.k: Automation increases expert work, Shipper argues
kp.d: Shipper argues that making existing expertise cheap generates additional demand for expert human judgment rather than eliminating expert knowledge work. His evidence comes principally from Every as an early-adopter workplace and examples in software and other knowledge work, not legal practice. He explicitly limits the employment argument: he does not claim automation creates more work for all jobs and acknowledges disruption as companies reorganize.
qs: There’s no tipping point coming where things flip and the jobs are gone. The new reality is the opposite—the more we automate, the more expert human work there is to do.

I’m not making an argument for why AI creates more work for *all* jobs. The economy is complicated, and what we have visibility into at Every is expert-level knowledge work—which is already being disrupted as companies reorganize around the new technology.

kp.k: Every reports extensive automation alongside continued human hiring
kp.d: Shipper reports that Every has almost 30 people, continues hiring customer-service staff, writers, editors and engineers, and retains SaaS products despite extensive AI use. Work allocation has changed: engineers no longer write code by hand, managers commit code, and engineers interact directly with customers. AI answered 95 percent of his work emails over the preceding several weeks, but he still reviewed email. These are company and personal observations rather than economy-wide employment findings.
qs: We are a team of almost 30 people, and we haven’t fired all of our employees in favor of agents.
We still hire humans to do customer service (with a lot of agent assistance), and we still hire human writers and editors and engineers.
Managers are committing code like ICs and engineers are talking directly to customers.
For the last several weeks, AI has responded to 95 percent of my work emails.

kp.k: Agent delegation and collaboration are distinct work modes
kp.d: Shipper distinguishes agents acting as employees, completing delegated tasks without the human in the immediate loop, from synchronous human-agent collaboration in Codex, Claude Code and Cowork. Employee agents include named coworkers handling proposals, editorial material and analysis, and embedded agents handling repetitive workflows. He considers shared-workspace collaboration more important for complex original work and says both modes require human involvement to work well.
qs: The first is the one the AI discourse predicted pretty well: agents as employees.
The second mode is stranger and, in my experience, more important. It is human-agent collaboration in tools like Codex, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork.
Agent employees are given a job, and go off to produce an answer, an action, a report, a draft, a triage decision, without you in the loop.
In both of these modes you can use AI to automate and delegate much of your work—and both of these modes require *you* or another human in order to work well.

kp.k: Support automation shifts humans toward systems and complex cases
kp.d: In a recent week in May, Every's embedded support agent Fin participated in 65 percent of 202 support conversations and closed 81 without human involvement, reported as 40.1 percent of all actionable conversations. Shipper says this lets customer-service manager Waqqas Mir devote less time to basic tickets and more to maintaining the response system and handling complex, high-touch cases.
qs: In a recent week in May, Fin participated in 65 percent of 202 Every support conversations and closed 81 of them without a human, which is 40.1 percent of all actionable conversations.

Embedded agents like this allow our customer service manager, Waqqas Mir, to spend less time responding to basic tickets, and more time building the system that responds to tickets and on complex cases that require high-touch interaction.

kp.k: Humans frame, check and operationalize agent work
kp.d: Shipper describes human responsibility at both ends of an agent task: choosing work, managing execution boundaries, reviewing quality, catching errors and turning outputs into decisions or processes. Engineers at Every consequently spend their time planning features and fixes, reviewing generated work and improving their working systems. This is an account of continuing human oversight rather than direct reliance on unattended outputs for complex tasks.
qs: Someone has to point it at the right thing, decide whether the output is good, catch the places where it is wrong, and turn the result into a real-life decision or process.
And you’re responsible for managing the agents at the start and end of each one of their tasks, making sure it’s done well, and finding the next piece of work to do.
We’ve found over and over that for any kind of complex task, the best way to get great work is to have an AI and a human going back and forth in the same workspace.

kp.k: Agent maintenance creates continuing engineering work
kp.d: Every initially gave each employee an agent but shifted to team-wide or company-wide agents because individual agents became stale when employees stopped maintaining them. Shipper reports a dedicated AI engineering team and expects continued need for it. One PowerPoint automation requires 24 skills and 18 scripts and costs $62 in tokens per deck, illustrating the maintenance and implementation burden behind apparently simple automation.
qs: Agents need a lot of maintenance, and personal agents quickly get stale when the employees they were working with gave up on them.
We have a team of AI engineers who are in charge of making sure our agents work well—and we’ll need them for the foreseeable future.
One of our PowerPoint automations includes 24 skills and 18 scripts and costs $62 in tokens to make a single deck.

kp.k: Cheap competence expands production across occupational boundaries
kp.d: Shipper argues that models package the recorded products of past human competence into inexpensive, widely accessible capabilities. At Every, operations and customer-service staff produce code, marketers create thumbnails, and engineers draft written material. As an external illustration of expanded output, he reports OpenClaw's 44,469 pull requests as of May 16, 2026, including 12,430 since April 1 and 3,990 since May 1, compared with Kubernetes's 5,200 in all of 2022.
qs: They take all of it—the exhaust of successfully completed tasks—and package it in a form that’s available to anyone, cheaply.
Operations and customer service people are writing code and issuing pull requests.
As of May 16, 2026, its repository had already seen 44,469 pull requests, including 12,430 since April 1 and 3,990 since May 1.

kp.k: Abundant generic output creates demand for differentiated expertise
kp.d: Shipper proposes an economic and cultural mechanism: shared models produce recognizable sameness, commoditizing default output as expectations rise. Users then seek context-specific, differentiated and higher-status work. He argues that human experts supply the live perspective needed to identify what matters now, while models can adopt that perspective after it is prompted. This is his theoretical explanation for continuing expert demand.
qs: Slop is visible sameness, repeated ad nauseam.
An abundance of sameness rapidly becomes a commodity.
When work is abundant and looks alike everywhere, the work that doesn’t fit the pattern becomes the rare, valuable, and high-status thing
Models can inhabit this perspective once it has been prompted, but not before.

kp.k: Experts absorb output and undertake more ambitious work
kp.d: Shipper describes two responses to expanded AI production: experts build review and quality-control systems, or use AI to do larger and more demanding projects themselves. Engineers review non-engineers' pull requests, designers improve marketers' thumbnails, and editors improve engineers' drafts. As an example of expanded capability, he reports that security firm Calif used Mythos Preview to find the first public macOS kernel memory exploit on Apple M5 hardware in five days, against his statement that finding operating-system vulnerabilities typically takes weeks or months.
qs: When operations people submit pull requests with AI, you need engineers to review them.

Some use AI to build systems that absorb and leverage the flood of new work: review queues, evals, harnesses, repo rules, Claude and Codex instruction files, continuous integration (CI), permissions, and workflows that turn first attempts into great work.
And some use AI to do bigger, more interesting, work than they could’ve done without it.

kp.k: Displacement warnings and benchmark gains motivate his counterargument
kp.d: Shipper reports, rather than endorses, Dario Amodei's warning that AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs. He acknowledges reported benchmark progress: Humanity's Last Exam rose from low single digits a year earlier to roughly 44 percent, GDPval to about 85 percent, and a May METR early Claude Mythos result achieved 80 percent success on tasks taking a human expert about 4 hours. He disputes the inference from such gains to wholesale job elimination.
qs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns that AI could wipe out up to half of all entry-level white-collar jobs
On Humanity’s Last Exam—a test of graduate-level reasoning—top models went from the low single digits a year ago to roughly 44 percent today.

In May, METR, an AI safety research nonprofit, released an early Claude Mythos result showing that the model had an 80 percent success rate on tasks that would take a human expert about 4 hours to complete.

kp.k: Internal coding benchmark measures performance within supplied framing
kp.d: Every's Senior Engineer benchmark asks agents to rewrite a problematic production codebase from Proof; Shipper compares outputs with two rewrites by human senior engineers using AI. GPT-5.5 scored 62/100 on its best run, about 30 points above Opus 4.7, while human senior engineers score in the high 80s or low 90s. He predicts models will reach the 80s and 90s within the next year, but emphasizes that scores depend on the prompt, harness and human-supplied framing.
qs: I also have two rewrites from human senior engineers, who used AI, that I use to compare and grade the model output.
GPT-5.5 scored a 62/100 on its best run—about 30 points above Opus 4.7.
My guess is that the models will hit the 80s and 90s on this benchmark within the next year.
It is a measure of the model inside a frame: the way it responds to a particular prompt.

kp.k: Benchmark saturation shifts demand toward wider contextual judgment
kp.d: Shipper argues that benchmarks freeze problems into measurable frames and that altered prompts can sharply lower or raise scores. He predicts that cheap codebase rewrites will multiply attempted projects, generating expert work on whether to rewrite, scope, preservation, migration, review and rollback. Once the current benchmark saturates, Every plans to broaden it to those decisions. His proposed recurring cycle is that automation cheapens framed tasks while revealing additional contextual work.
qs: To measure anything, you have to freeze a problem into a static—and therefore measurable—frame.
If we replaced the prompt entirely with one asking the model to “solve all of the errors that keep popping up,” the model’s score would be close to zero.
Once the benchmark starts to saturate, the work inside its frame gets cheaper. Demand for experts who can adapt that newly cheap competence to today’s live problems goes up.

The next benchmark will not ask only, “Can you rewrite the app?” It will ask: Can you decide when a rewrite is needed, choose the scope, preserve the right invariants, manage the migration, and judge whether the result is any good?

kp.k: GDPval embeds human judgment before models start
kp.d: Shipper notes that GDPval includes occupations such as lawyers, compliance officers and software developers. He reports launch results of GPT-5 matching or exceeding professionals 40.6 percent of the time and Claude Opus 4.1 exceeding experts 49 percent of the time. Using an audit prompt specifying data, confidence level, sampling priorities and output format, he argues that these task results omit the expert judgment already invested in defining the assignment. He calls this hidden contribution 'smuggled intelligence'; he does not present separate findings about legal work.
qs: It evaluates how well AI performs expert-level tasks from various occupations like compliance officers, lawyers, software developers, and more.
When GDPval first came out, OpenAI’s research showed that GPT-5 was as good as or better than human professionals 40.6 percent of the time.
There is an enormous amount of human intelligence going into framing this problem in a way that a model can complete.
The hard human work that GDPval does not measure has already been done before the model begins.

kp.k: AGI remains dependent on human ends in his framework
kp.d: Shipper proposes an operational definition of AGI as an agent economically worth running continuously, thinking, learning and acting 24/7; he says current systems are nowhere near that condition. He speculates that even AGI capable of repeatedly choosing frames will pursue a supplied goal, reward or progress signal, leaving humans to determine what matters. He distinguishes task autonomy from independently wanting and choosing ends, and conditions his argument on agents not becoming ends in themselves acting independently of human wishes.
qs: Once I have a persistent system that I pay to keep thinking, learning, and acting 24/7, I think that will decisively look like AGI.
This AGI can choose and re-choose frames, but only in pursuit of some goal it has been given, some reward it is optimizing, or some signal someone has decided should count as progress

Unless and until they become ends in themselves—pursuing their own goals, moving between them fluently, deciding to do things independently of, without reference to, and *despite the wishes of*, any human operator—the situation doesn’t change.
Model compliance and helpfulness are fundamentally at odds with this kind of agency, so even as the models improve, the gap between models and humans will remain.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dan Shipper argues that automation increases demand for expert human knowledge work by expanding output and creating new needs for judgment, differentiation, supervision, and system-building.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain account of knowledge work, principally software engineering, writing, design, operations, and customer service, rather than a claim specifically about legal services. Shipper distinguishes asynchronous agents that execute delegated, repeatable tasks from interactive human-agent collaboration for complex, original work. He says both require human direction and oversight. His proposed mechanism is that AI makes established competence cheap, more people use it, generic output proliferates, and experts become more valuable for adapting that output to specific circumstances. Experts both build systems to manage the resulting work and undertake more ambitious projects themselves. He further argues that benchmark gains measure performance within human-supplied problem frames, not the replacement of the humans who determine what matters. He predicts that this demand-generating cycle will continue even under his definition of AGI, provided systems remain directed toward human ends.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Shipper supports his claims with Every’s operating experience, selected usage and output figures, an in-house engineering benchmark, external benchmark reports, and a conceptual account of commoditization and human problem-framing.
pts.d: Every is presented as an early-adopter laboratory of almost 30 people that continues hiring humans despite extensive automation. Shipper reports that AI responded to 95 percent of his work emails over several weeks while he still reviewed them. In a May week, the embedded support agent Fin participated in 65 percent of 202 conversations and closed 81 without a human. Agent-maintenance experience includes abandoning individual employee agents in favor of shared agents, employing AI engineers to maintain them, and a PowerPoint automation requiring 24 skills, 18 scripts, and $62 in tokens per deck. To illustrate expanding output, he reports 44,469 OpenClaw pull requests by May 16, 2026, compared with 5,200 Kubernetes pull requests in 2022. His Senior Engineer benchmark uses a real troubled Proof codebase and two human senior engineers’ AI-assisted rewrites as comparators: GPT-5.5 scored 62/100 on its best run, approximately 30 points above Opus 4.7, versus human scores in the high 80s or low 90s. He uses prompt sensitivity and a detailed GDPval audit task to argue that benchmark achievements incorporate substantial prior human judgment. He also cites Calif’s reported five-day macOS exploit discovery using Mythos Preview as an example of experts accomplishing more with AI. The enduring-demand and AGI claims are advanced through this experience and conceptual argument, rather than through an economy-wide employment study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account combines current observations in 2026, a one-year engineering-benchmark forecast, and a longer-term conditional prediction extending to AGI.
pts.d: Shipper describes Every’s adoption of Claude Code from mid-2025 and reports recent operational experience and May 2026 activity. He expects models to score in the 80s and 90s on Every’s current Senior Engineer benchmark within the next year. His GPT-6 rewrite example is conditional: if rewrites become push-button tasks, he predicts more rewrites and more expert work determining scope, timing, migration, and review. He expressly limits his employment argument to expert-level knowledge work, acknowledges disruption and company reorganization, and does not claim that automation increases work across all jobs. For the longer term, he defines AGI operationally as a persistent system worth paying to keep thinking, learning, and acting continuously, says this has not yet arrived, and argues that human framing remains necessary even then. This conclusion is conditional on systems continuing to pursue human-specified ends rather than independently pursuing their own ends.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Shipper describes changing work for expert practitioners, non-specialists using newly accessible skills, managers, support staff, and organizations maintaining agents.
pts.d: Engineers shift from manually writing code toward planning, reviewing agent work, improving workflows, and deciding how technical changes fit business needs. Operations and customer-service staff can submit code, marketers can produce thumbnails, and engineers can draft written material, generating downstream work for engineers, designers, writers, and editors. Customer-service staff spend less time on basic tickets and more on system-building and complex, high-touch cases. Managers can contribute code, while engineers interact directly with customers. AI engineers maintain shared agents and their supporting infrastructure. Founders, product managers, operations personnel, and junior engineers are prospective users of cheaper codebase rewrites, with senior engineers handling the surrounding decisions. Lawyers appear only among the occupations represented in GDPval; the source does not offer separate findings about legal employment, law-firm staffing, legal pricing, or access to justice.
